transistor-bias-calculator.name: Transistor Bias Calculator
transistor-bias-calculator.tagline: Find the Q-point of a voltage-divider biased BJT: IC, VCE, VB, VE, and stability.
transistor-bias-calculator.metaTitle: Transistor Bias Calculator – BJT Q-Point Finder | JaurTools
transistor-bias-calculator.metaDescription: Free BJT transistor bias calculator. Enter VCC, divider resistors, RC, RE and beta to get IC, VCE and the operating point — 100% in your browser.
transistor-bias-calculator.keywords: transistor bias calculator, BJT bias calculator, voltage divider bias, Q point calculator, base bias
transistor-bias-calculator.quickAnswer: The base voltage is set by the R1–R2 divider: VB = VCC × R2/(R1+R2). Subtract the 0.7 V base–emitter drop to get VE, divide by RE for the emitter current (IC ≈ IE), then VCE = VCC − IC×(RC+RE). With 12 V, 47k/10k, RC 2.2k, RE 1k, β 100: IC ≈ 1.41 mA and VCE ≈ 7.50 V — solidly in the active region.
keyFacts: Voltage-divider bias is the most stable common biasing method: the divider fixes VB nearly independent of β.
The Q-point (quiescent point) is the DC operating point — IC and VCE with no input signal.
Approximation used: VBE = 0.7 V for silicon, and IC ≈ IE (ignoring the small base current).
Active region needs VCE above ~0.2 V; near zero the transistor saturates and stops amplifying linearly.
Stability rule of thumb: R2 ≤ β×RE/10 keeps the divider stiff against β variation between transistors.
IC(sat) = VCC/(RC+RE) is the maximum possible collector current — your Q-point IC must stay well below it.
howTo: Enter the divider resistors R1 (top) and R2 (bottom) in kΩ.
Enter the collector resistor RC and emitter resistor RE in kΩ.
Enter the transistor's current gain β (hFE) from its datasheet.
Read IC, VCE, the node voltages, saturation current, region, and stability check.
transistor-bias-calculator.formula:
VB = VCC × R2/(R1+R2)
VE = VB − 0.7 V
IE = VE/RE,  IC ≈ IE
VCE = VCC − IC×(RC+RE)
IC(sat) = VCC/(RC+RE)
Stable if R2 ≤ β×RE/10
transistor-bias-calculator.workedExample:
VCC 12 V, R1 47 kΩ, R2 10 kΩ, RC 2.2 kΩ, RE 1 kΩ, β 100.
VB = 12 × 10/57 = 2.11 V
VE = 2.11 − 0.7 = 1.41 V
IC ≈ IE = 1.41/1 = 1.405 mA
VCE = 12 − 1.405 × 3.2 = 7.50 V
IC(sat) = 12/3.2 = 3.75 mA — operating current is well below it.
VCE > 0.2 V → active region. R2 = 10 kΩ ≤ β×RE/10 = 10 kΩ → stable bias.
benefits: Designs a working amplifier bias point in seconds — no manual algebra.
Flags saturation and unstable dividers before you solder anything.
Shows every node voltage, so you know what to expect on a multimeter.
Teaches the classic analysis steps while it computes.
limitations: Uses the approximate analysis (VBE = 0.7 V, IC ≈ IE) — fine for design, not a SPICE replacement.
Assumes an NPN silicon transistor at room temperature; germanium or PNP needs sign adjustments.
Ignores Early effect, temperature drift of VBE, and β variation with current.
DC bias only: AC gain, input/output impedance, and frequency response need separate small-signal analysis.
An educational design aid — verify critical circuits by measurement.

faqs.a: The quiescent (no-signal) DC operating point of the transistor, described by IC and VCE. A good Q-point sits in the active region with headroom for the signal swing.
A forward-biased silicon base–emitter junction drops about 0.7 V, so the emitter sits 0.7 V below the base: VE = VB − 0.7 V.

faqs.q: Why is IC approximately equal to IE?
faqs.a: The emitter current splits into collector current plus a small base current (IE = IC + IB). Since IB = IC/β is tiny for β ≥ 50, IC ≈ IE is an excellent approximation.
If VCE falls near zero, the collector–base junction forward-biases and the transistor saturates — it acts like a closed switch instead of a linear amplifier.

faqs.q: What is a stiff voltage divider?
faqs.a: A divider whose current is much larger than the base current, so VB barely moves when β varies. The rule R2 ≤ β×RE/10 is the standard check.

faqs.q: Can I use this for PNP transistors?
faqs.a: The magnitudes work the same, but polarities reverse (VEE negative, currents flow out). This tool presents the NPN convention — flip signs for PNP.

labels.dividerHint: R1 connects VCC to the base node; R2 connects the base node to ground.
labels.reHint: RE provides negative feedback that stabilizes the bias point.
labels.betaHint: From the transistor datasheet; typical 100–300 for small-signal BJTs.
labels.stableNo: Unstable — lower R2 or raise RE
labels.assumptionNoteText: Assumes NPN silicon at room temperature: VBE = 0.7 V and IC ≈ IE.
